title: Under his wings (Psalm 91)
hookLine: he shall cover you with his feathers
carry: warm and dark and loud with heartbeats

cards: A shadow crosses the farmyard: a hawk, circling low. The hen doesn't run. She makes one sharp sound, and every chick within earshot comes skittering across the dirt and disappears under her.
In two seconds there's no chick to be seen, only a hen who suddenly looks twice her size, feathers puffed, eyes on the sky. Underneath, it's warm and dark and loud with heartbeats.
The writers of the Bible had seen it too, and they used it for God, in a psalm said at night.

teach.b: The psalm opens, in the King James Bible: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."
Then, verse four: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust."

teach.h: KANAF: A WING, A CLOAK'S EDGE
teach.b: The Hebrew word for wing is kanaf. It also means the edge of a cloak. In the book of Ruth, Boaz blesses Ruth, the foreigner who has come to Israel, as one who has come to trust under the wings of the God of Israel.
Later, at night, Ruth asks Boaz to spread his kanaf, his cloak, over her, and the King James Bible translates it skirt. Wings and a cloak: both are ways of saying you're covered, you belong.
The psalm goes on: "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day." That's one reason it belongs to the night.
It is part of Jewish bedtime prayers, and some churches pray it at Compline, the last service of the day. But the psalm can be misused.
In the Gospels, when the devil tempts Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple, he quotes this very psalm: he shall give his angels charge over thee. Go on, jump.
And Jesus answers, "It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God."
The psalm is a place to hide, not a dare to take.

teach.h: UNDER HIS WINGS SHALT THOU TRUST.
teach.b: And Jesus used the same farmyard picture himself, over Jerusalem: how often would I have gathered thy children together, "even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."

how: Psalm 91 is a night psalm for many Christians: it is prayed at Compline in Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran traditions, and many people pray it for protection before travel, surgery or military service.

games.q: you're Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple. the devil quotes Psalm 91: the angels will catch you. go on, jump. what do you say?
o: jump, to prove the psalm true.
it is written again, thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.
games.why: Jesus answers with another verse of scripture. the psalm is for trusting, not for testing God.

practice: Bring to mind one person who could use covering right now, someone traveling, someone sick, someone scared, a kid walking into a hard week, and picture where they are.
If you pray, ask God to cover them with his feathers, or simply say their name to God and leave it there. If you don't, hold them in mind and wish them safe, steadily, the way a hen sits still.

wordCard.voice: Kanaf. Hebrew for wing, also the edge of a cloak, Psalm ninety-one's picture of God as a bird sheltering its young, a psalm for the night.
